html:
The walled park of altars and halls in the south of Beijing where the emperors of China prayed to Heaven for good harvests. It was built from 1406 to 1420 by the Yongle Emperor of the Ming, in the same years as the Forbidden City.

The emperor was the Son of Heaven, and the harvest was the test of his right to rule. Each year at the winter solstice he came in procession, fasted, and made offerings on the open Circular Mound Altar. In spring he prayed in the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests, a round wooden hall 38 metres high, with three roofs of blue tile, built without nails.

The plan follows an old idea: Heaven is round and Earth is square. So the halls and altars are round and stand on square bases, and the outer wall is curved at the north and straight at the south. The Qing emperors kept up the rites until 1911.
